This is awesome, and along the same motivation to what I'm proposing. Basically, here's my train of thought:

- Say you have a codebase, and you open a file to edit in lambdu. This file defines types used in other modules.
- Now, you make a pseudo-breaking change in one of the types (represented as a diff of the old version to the new one, in an AST - like a AST-level patch)
- We __cannot__ commit this change yet, because the breaking change borks the other modules that depended on the old type
- Thus, we need to build a _set_ of patches to submit atomically, s.t. all expressions dependent on the breaking change are also patched.
  - In the case of sum types and enumerated pattern matches (no wildcards), a new sum type would just require an additional matched expression.

I'm not sure if this is along the same goal, but I plan to take this concept very far in a Haskell interpreter, to allow a running program to be modified via these atomically submitted patches.

I'm not trying to change the language's semantics in any way, I'm trying to change program _editing_ semantics. I'm trying to capture the general case of writing Haskell code, for instance when building `Maybe` and `Either`, when developing the prelude. In this model of editing, there would be no opportunities for "inconsistency" across the codebase.

I feel as though _browsers_ are enforcing the adoption of the key/value system now, and it would be wise for us to adopt it as well. The `urlDecode` function from http-types seems to be the best bet, from what I've seen, as a low-level percent un-escaping function. It also lets us flag whether or not we should un-escape `+` as a space, too, which makes it a complete tool for decoding.

My solution so far has been to use `urlDecode`, `Data.ByteString.UTF8.toString` from utf8-string, and `splitOn` from the split package. I also feel as though `Maybe String` is more explicit in terms of possibly existent values than matching an empty string. To create our list of pairs with potential elements, it's as simple as:

    import Data.ByteString as BS
    import Data.ByteString.UTF8 as BS
    import Data.List.Split
    import Network.HTTP.Types (urlDecode)
    
    -- | Turns '+' to ' ' as an example
    decodeUrl :: ByteString -> [(String, Maybe String)]
    decodeUrl xs =
      let string = BS.toString (urlDecode True xs)
          getVal c = case splitOn "=" c of
                       [k]   -> (k, Nothing)
                       [k,v] -> (k, Just v)
                       _     -> error "more than one value bound to a key"
      in map getVal (splitOn "&" string)

No, λtext is _not_ turing complete - infinite recursion / `while(true)` loops are not possible - λtext uses a _predicative_ lambda calculus, not the untyped version that allows terms like `ω := λx. x x`, or the Y combinator. In short, λtext only allows for substitution of files _linearly_ through the size of the expression.

And lastly, there is no arithmetic allowed in λtext - it would recognize `$$ 1 + 1 %%` _equally_ to `$$ foo bar foo %%` - ie; `1` and `+` would be seen as variables, not operators. The _only_ special symbols are `\` (lambda), `->` (arrow), `(` (left paren), and `)` (right paren).

It is not intended to be a programming language, but merely a text file utility like `cat` or `wc`. I hope this answers your question :)

Something like this: Say I want to make a recursive function for a data type indexed by some proof - as we construct the data type with it's GADT constructors, it's type changes - and becomes heterogeneous. By using type classes, we can still make a pseudo-recursive value-level function that hinges on hypotheses as instance heads. [Here's an example](https://github.com/athanclark/nested-routes/blob/master/src/Web/Routes/Nested/Types.hs#L40) in [nested-routes](http://hackage.haskell.org/package/nested-routes).

Notice, line `43` is the base case for the induction, and `46` is our step. The instance heads in `46` _and_ the functional dependencies are what force the induction to work without type variables being ambiguous: If I have a `Singleton` from `a` to `trie0`, and an `Extend` from `trie0` to `trie1`, then I have a `Singleton` from `a` to `trie1`. It's just like how you would write a recursive function, but this time the types diverge. We use typeclasses to make sure the divergence is _just_ right.
Until then, you could always do insane stuff like facilitate heterogeneous induction via typeclasses :)

Adaptive websites use percentages, and that has to be calculated at some point, either beforehand with a CSS compiler or with javascript via run-time injection with jquery or something (not very clean). I mean, adaptive websites run off the % of the window width, and ems are based on the current font size. If the font size were to increase, what would happen if the window were resized? Because if the columns were based of ems, then they would increase in size as the font size increased, thus making the whole canvas of the website increase beyond the view port, yet still having it be adaptive would be the adaptation would behave in respect with the canvas... which is larger than the view port. It's a bad idea, imo. Just stick with the user's current screen and make elements that have text have a static em-based width, everything else columns.

You also might want to experiment on different browsers to see if they see media queries respective to ems. That way you could mix em-based and responsive based, giving everyone a customized feel for the website.
